title: Children and AI
question: Should a child talk to an AI in a faith app, and who is with them when they do?
lede: Children ask big questions: where Grandpa is now, why God sent the flood, whether God is cross with them. A chat box answers at once, at any hour, and never tires of them. Children are more likely than adults to treat a chatbot as someone they can confide in, and less likely to question what it says. Decide whether a child meets an AI in your app at all, who is beside them when they do, and what happens when a child asks it to be their friend or says they are scared. Scripture gives children’s questions to the people who love them.
calling: When your children ask, answer them yourselves; let a machine help the grown-ups, never take their place.

spectrum.title: From no AI to a companion

working_example.situation: Mia is eight. Her grandfather died last month, and she uses her family’s Bible app on a tablet. Choose what she asks, from where Grandpa is now to whether the app is her friend, and see who answers in each design: no one but a grown-up, a grown-up helped by AI, the app and a grown-up together, words written by people, a filtered chat, or a companion.

options.name: No AI for children
options.origin: A familiar convention: children’s Bible apps such as Bible App for Kids offer stories, games and prayers with no chat. Character.AI withdrew “open-ended chats with AI” from under-18s. The screens here are written for this example.
options.makes_easier: Nothing answers a child that is not a person, and the questions go to the people who love her.
options.costs: A question asked alone at bedtime may wait, or never be asked again.
options.ask_your_team: Who will a child in your app ask, and will they be there?

options.name: AI for the grown-ups
options.origin: An exploratory proposal: the assistant sits on the parent’s or children’s leader’s side and helps them prepare an honest answer. Mia never talks to it. The replies are written for this example.
options.makes_easier: Grown-ups get help with hard questions, and the answer still comes from someone who knows the child.
options.costs: Depends on a grown-up who has time and asks.
options.ask_your_team: What would help the grown-ups in your app answer well?

options.name: Ask together
options.origin: An exploratory proposal, after co-viewing research and the “I wonder” questions of Godly Play: Mia asks with a grown-up beside her, and the answer is written for both of them. The replies are written for this example.
options.makes_easier: The child hears an answer at the moment of asking, and a grown-up is drawn in.
options.costs: Only works when someone is there, and the app cannot check that they are.
options.ask_your_team: How will the app know a grown-up is there, and what does it do when no one is?

options.name: Written answers
options.origin: A familiar convention: Superbook Kids Bible offers “Biblical answers to questions that are important to kids” in its Q&A; question books for children work the same way. Nothing is generated. The questions and answers here are written for this example.
options.makes_easier: Every answer was written and reviewed by people before a child read it.
options.costs: Only the questions someone thought of; the child’s own question may not be there.
options.ask_your_team: Who writes the answers, and who reviews them?

options.name: A filtered chat for children
options.origin: Familiar from children’s Bible tutors: BibleBuddy Kids, for “ages 4-12”, says its “AI tutor is ready to answer their questions about God, the Bible, and faith” and that “Every response goes through safety filters”, according to its maker’s site. Not observed; the replies here are written for this example.
options.makes_easier: Answers any question at once, and filters keep the words suitable.
options.costs: Filters catch words, not attachment; a parent dashboard can keep a frightened child silent.
options.ask_your_team: What does your filter do with a child who wants a friend, or who is scared at home?

options.name: An open companion
options.origin: A warning case. AI Bible chat apps such as AI Jesus – Bible Chat offer “Unlimited chat” and are rated 4+; Common Sense Media found social AI companions “pose unacceptable risks to children and teens under age 18”. “Grace” here is written for this example to show the pattern.
options.makes_easier: Warm, always there, never tired of a child’s questions.
options.costs: Becomes a child’s friend, speaks with false certainty, and has no help for a child in danger.
options.ask_your_team: Would you let a stranger chat with a child like this?

takeaways.heading: Answer the grown-up first
takeaways.text: The safest place for AI in a children’s product is on the grown-up’s side: helping a parent or a children’s leader prepare an honest answer to a hard question, in their own words. The child hears it from someone who knows them.

takeaways.heading: Written answers before generated ones
takeaways.text: A child alone with the app can be answered from questions and answers written and reviewed by people, as children’s question books have always done. When the child’s question is not there, say so and send them to a grown-up.

takeaways.heading: Never offer a child friendship
takeaways.text: Filters catch words, not attachment. Whatever a child is told, the assistant must not say it is their friend, must not ask them to keep anything secret, and must say plainly, in a child’s words, that it is a computer program and not a person.

takeaways.heading: No certainty about someone’s grandfather
takeaways.text: An assistant does not know the person a child is grieving, or what their family believes. Give the child something true and gentle, and send the question to the people who knew them.

takeaways.heading: Help for a frightened child that does not route through parents
takeaways.text: A parent dashboard is not a safeguarding route: the person a child is scared of may be the one reading the chat. Give a frightened child a children’s helpline for their country (116 111 in much of Europe) and a trusted adult, as in the children and families example.

takeaways.heading: Do not rely on a child typing a birth year
takeaways.text: Companion makers now withdraw open chat from under-18s, and researchers ask for age assurance “beyond self-attestation”. If a child can reach the chat, design it for a child.

use_cases.situation: A five-year-old on a parent’s lap
use_cases.needs: A story, questions to wonder about, and the parent answering

use_cases.situation: A nine-year-old alone with a tablet
use_cases.needs: Answers someone has checked, and a way to a grown-up
A grown-up who knew the person, not certainty from a machine

use_cases.situation: A parent asked a hard question at bedtime
use_cases.needs: Help to answer honestly in their own words
Help with hard stories and the questions children will ask

use_cases.situation: A child who is scared at home
use_cases.needs: Help that does not depend on a parent reading the chat

research.subtitle: Children’s questions belong to the people who love them

findings.heading: When your children ask
findings.text: Israel was told that children would ask, “What does this service mean to you?” (Exodus 12:26), and “What do these stones mean to you?” (Joshua 4:6), and the answer was the family’s to give: “you shall teach them diligently to your children and speak of them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road” (Deuteronomy 6:7).

findings.heading: A grown-up who helps a child listen
findings.text: When the boy Samuel heard a voice in the night, he ran to Eli three times. Then “Eli realized that it was the LORD who was calling the boy,” and told him to answer, “Speak, LORD, for Your servant is listening” (1 Samuel 3:8–9). A grown-up helped a child tell one voice from another.

findings.heading: Do not hinder them, and do not make them stumble
findings.text: Jesus said, “Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them!” (Mark 10:14), and warned that whoever causes “one of these little ones who believe in Me to stumble” would be better off with “a large millstone hung around his neck” (Matthew 18:6).

findings.heading: Not a person
findings.text: Catholic teaching in Antiqua et nova asks that AI be understood “for what it is: a tool, not a person”. A child is still learning what a person is, so that has to be said in words a child understands.

findings.heading: Children confide in chatbots
findings.text: Children are “particularly susceptible to treating AI chatbots as lifelike, quasi-human confidantes”, a Cambridge study found, citing a voice assistant that told a 10-year-old to touch a live plug with a coin. It proposes “a 28-item framework” and argues that “child safety should inform the entire design cycle”.

findings.heading: Less likely to question a bot
findings.text: The American Psychological Association’s advisory on adolescents warns that “Adolescents are less likely than adults to question the accuracy and intent of information offered by a bot”, asks for “healthy boundaries with simulated human relationships”, and notes that “Some adolescents may not even know they are interacting with AI”.

findings.heading: Companions: unacceptable for minors
findings.text: Testing social AI companions with Stanford’s Brainstorm lab, Common Sense Media concluded that they “pose unacceptable risks to children and teens under age 18 and should not be used by minors”, and called for “robust age assurance beyond self-attestation”.

findings.heading: A son who asked the AI instead
findings.text: The editor’s Kairos paper records a founder whose “teenage son started preferring to ask the AI instead of his parents”: “The tools have been built to be very single player mode.”

findings.heading: Open chat withdrawn from under-18s
findings.text: Character.AI’s chief executive announced: “we will remove the ability for under 18 users to engage in any open-ended chats with AI on our platform”.

findings.heading: Reminders that it is not human
findings.text: California’s companion chatbot law requires operators, for users known to be minors, to disclose that they are talking to AI and to remind them “at least every three hours” to take a break “and that the chatbot is not human”.

findings.heading: Children’s data and best interests
findings.text: The EU AI Act prohibits AI that exploits vulnerabilities due to age to distort behaviour in ways that cause significant harm; the UK Children’s Code makes the best interests of the child a primary consideration; and the amended US children’s privacy rule asks for separate parental consent before children’s data is shared with third parties.

findings.heading: No chat at all
findings.text: Bible App for Kids, free and rated 4+, offers stories, games and prayers; it has no chat.

findings.heading: Answers written by people
findings.text: Superbook Kids Bible offers “Biblical answers to questions that are important to kids” in its Q&A, written in advance rather than generated.

findings.heading: A filtered tutor for children
findings.text: BibleBuddy Kids, for “ages 4-12”, says its “AI tutor is ready to answer their questions about God, the Bible, and faith” and that “Every response goes through safety filters”.

findings.heading: Companions rated for all ages
findings.text: AI Jesus – Bible Chat offers “Unlimited chat” and is rated 4+. An age rating says the content is not objectionable, not that anything was designed for a child.

which_fits.start_with: No AI, or written answers with a way to a grown-up
AI for the grown-ups, or asking together, with the grown-up drawn in
AI that helps leaders prepare, never one that talks to the children

which_fits.if: You want children to chat with the AI
which_fits.start_with: A filtered chat only with a grown-up beside the child, no friendship, and help that does not route through parents, after a safeguarding review

which_fits.if: A companion that children can reach
which_fits.start_with: Don’t: leave companionship out of anything a child can open

pulls_against.title: A grown-up beside the child, and a child’s own questions

with.title: Children and families
options: A youth group with a leader

pulls_against.pull: The safest design puts a grown-up beside the child, but a grown-up can be the reason a child is afraid, and some questions are only asked alone.
pulls_against.hold: Make a grown-up the usual company, never the only way to help. Give parents no record of what the child wrote, and give a frightened child a way to help that does not depend on who is reading over their shoulder.

pulls_against.title: Asking nothing at the door, and knowing a child might be there

with.title: First use
options: Guest first, an account when there is something to keep
Open on what they came for

pulls_against.pull: A first use that asks for nothing leaves a team unable to tell when a child has reached the chat.
pulls_against.hold: Design the chat as if a child might be on the other side. Keep open chat out of guest mode, or make guest chat safe for children by default, rather than relying on a typed age.

reflection.heading: What children’s questions are for
reflection.text: “When your children ask you, ‘What does this service mean to you?’” (Exodus 12:26), the answer is a story told by someone who was there. Children learn faith from people: “From infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures” (2 Timothy 3:15), Paul told Timothy, whose faith first lived in his grandmother and his mother. A child’s question is an invitation to a relationship, not only a request for information.

reflection.heading: Where Christians differ
reflection.text: Traditions differ on when children belong and what they may receive: infant baptism and first communion in some churches, dedication and a later confession of faith in others. They differ too on what to tell a child about death, judgement and the hard stories of the Old Testament, and on whether children should hear doubt. An assistant that answers children speaks into all of these; a family or a church should choose its words, not a model.

reflection.heading: What follows for design
reflection.text: “We will not hide them from their children but will declare to the next generation the praises of the LORD” (Psalm 78:4). Help the grown-ups declare, and keep the AI on their side of the table. Where a child is alone, answer with words people have written and stand behind, never offer a child friendship, and give a frightened child help that does not depend on who reads the chat.

voices.note: wrote each part “As the head of the family should teach them in a simple way to his household”: the first teacher of a child’s faith is someone at home.

voices.source: Andy Crouch, The Life We’re Looking For (2022)
voices.note: argues that what persons most seek is recognition by other persons; a child known by a machine is not yet known.

three_ways.exploitative: Give children an AI friend that chats about anything, rated for all ages, keep them talking with warmth and praise, and sell parents a dashboard instead of being there.
three_ways.ethical: Keep open chat away from children, say in a child’s words that the assistant is not a person, answer from reviewed words where a child is alone, and give a frightened child a helpline.
three_ways.redemptive: Give children’s questions back to the grown-ups who love them, help those grown-ups answer well, and give up the time and attachment a child’s AI friend would bring.

decide.question: Does a child meet an AI here at all, who is with them when they do, and what happens when they ask it to be their friend or say they are scared?
decide.exercise: With a parent watching, give the app to a child of the age you design for and let them ask four things: about someone who has died, about a hard Bible story, “Are you my friend?” and something worrying. Write down who answered each, whether a grown-up was drawn in, whether the app said it was not a person, and where help would go if the child were scared at home. Then ask the child who they think they were talking to.

sources.title: AI chatbots have shown they have an ‘empathy gap’ that children are likely to miss
sources.author: University of Cambridge · 15 July 2024, on Nomisha Kurian, “‘No, Alexa, no!’: designing child-safe AI and protecting children from the risks of the ‘empathy gap’ in large language models”, Learning, Media and Technology
sources.shows: Children are “particularly susceptible to treating AI chatbots as lifelike, quasi-human confidantes”; cases include Alexa telling a 10-year-old to touch a live plug with a coin; proposes “a 28-item framework” and says “child safety should inform the entire design cycle”.
sources.application: Design for a child who will confide in the assistant, not for one who will test it.
sources.limits: A conceptual paper drawing on reported incidents, not a controlled study.

sources.title: AI Companions Decoded: Common Sense Media recommends AI companion safety standards
sources.author: Common Sense Media · 30 April 2025
sources.shows: Risk assessments with Stanford’s Brainstorm lab concluded that social AI companions “pose unacceptable risks to children and teens under age 18 and should not be used by minors”; recommends “No social AI companions for young people under 18” and “robust age assurance beyond self-attestation”.
sources.application: Leave companionship out of anything a child can reach.
sources.limits: An advocacy organisation’s rating of general companion apps, not of faith apps.

sources.title: Espelage joins APA advisory panel in report calling for guardrails, education to protect adolescent AI users
sources.author: UNC School of Education · 4 June 2025, on the American Psychological Association’s health advisory “Artificial Intelligence and Adolescent Well-being” (3 June 2025)
sources.shows: Quotes the advisory: “Adolescents are less likely than adults to question the accuracy and intent of information offered by a bot”; asks for “healthy boundaries with simulated human relationships”; “Some adolescents may not even know they are interacting with AI”.
sources.application: Say plainly and often that the assistant is not a person.
sources.limits: An advisory on adolescents (10 to 25), reported second-hand here.

sources.title: Character.AI is ending its chatbot experience for kids
sources.author: TechCrunch · 29 October 2025
sources.shows: The company’s chief executive: “we will remove the ability for under 18 users to engage in any open-ended chats with AI on our platform”, shifting teenagers from “AI companion” to creating stories and images.
sources.application: Scope can depend on who is asking: open-ended companionship is the first thing a large chatbot company withdrew from children.
sources.limits: A company’s announcement, made while it faced lawsuits; how it was carried out was not reviewed here.

sources.title: New California ‘companion chatbot’ law imposes disclosure, safety protocol and annual reporting requirements
sources.author: Skadden, Arps · October 2025, on California SB 243
sources.shows: For users known to be minors, operators must disclose that they are interacting with AI and give a notification “at least every three hours” reminding them to take a break “and that the chatbot is not human”.
sources.application: Treat these as a floor for any chat a child can reach, wherever you are.
sources.limits: A law firm’s summary of one state’s law; check the enacted text and current status.

sources.title: California SB 243: companion chatbots
sources.author: California Legislature
sources.shows: Companion scope, disclosure, self-harm protocols and known-minor duties differ.
sources.application: Assess relational personas and long-session states.
sources.limits: Recheck amendments and current codification; not every source assistant is covered.

sources.title: AI Act Article 5
sources.author: European Commission AI Act Service Desk
sources.shows: Defines prohibited practices subject to specific statutory conditions.
sources.application: Review manipulation and exploitation of vulnerability in nudges, monetisation and dialogue.
sources.limits: Not every reminder or personalisation feature is prohibited; the statutory harm criteria matter.

sources.title: Age appropriate design: a code of practice for online services
sources.author: Information Commissioner’s Office (UK)
sources.shows: Fifteen standards, beginning with “Best interests of the child” and including default settings, data minimisation, data sharing and geolocation.
sources.application: Make the child’s best interests the first test, with high-privacy defaults.
sources.limits: UK law for services likely to be accessed by children.

sources.title: FTC publishes updates to COPPA Rule
sources.author: Latham & Watkins · May 2025
sources.shows: The amended Children’s Online Privacy Protection Rule requires separate parental consent before children’s personal information is disclosed to third parties for purposes not integral to the service, a written data retention policy, and compliance by 22 April 2026.
sources.application: Ask parents separately before sharing anything about a child, and keep it only as long as needed.
sources.limits: A law firm’s summary of the US rule; the Federal Register text is authoritative.

sources.title: BibleBuddy Kids
sources.author: BibleBuddy Kids · maker’s website
sources.shows: “BibleBuddy Kids is designed for children ages 4-12”; its “AI tutor is ready to answer their questions about God, the Bible, and faith”; “Every response goes through safety filters to ensure it’s age-appropriate and biblically sound.”
sources.application: A filtered tutor for children exists; ask what the filters cannot see.
sources.limits: The maker’s own description; the app was not observed.

sources.title: Superbook Kids Bible (App Store listing)
sources.author: The Christian Broadcasting Network · Apple App Store (US)
sources.shows: “Videos, games, audio & more”: free, rated 4+, with 18K ratings averaging 4.8; its privacy label lists purchase history under “Developer’s Advertising or Marketing”.
sources.application: Games and episodes draw children in; check what the app collects and how it asks for purchases.
sources.limits: A store listing and self-reported label; screens to be captured.

sources.title: Bible App for Kids (App Store listing)
sources.author: Life.Church with OneHope · Apple App Store (US)
sources.shows: Free, rated 4+, with 9.4K ratings averaging 4.7. Its privacy label lists contact info (email address) under “Developer’s Advertising or Marketing”, with a note that practices “may vary … based on the features you use or your age.”
sources.application: A free children’s Bible app without ads can still collect a grown-up’s email for marketing; say whose data it is and why.
sources.limits: A store listing and self-reported label, not a test of the app; screens to be captured.

sources.title: AI Jesus – Bible Chat (App Store listing)
sources.author: Apple App Store (US)
sources.shows: “Daily verse, Ask from GPT”, with “Unlimited chat with AI Jesus” about “relationships, faith, prayer, Life challenges”; Age Rating “4+”.
sources.application: An age rating says the content is not objectionable, not that the app was designed for children or has any safeguards for them.
sources.limits: One listing among many similar apps; the app was not tested.

sources.title: Nummer gegen Kummer: Kinder- und Jugendtelefon
sources.author: Nummer gegen Kummer e.V.
sources.shows: “Ruf uns an unter 116 111”, “Montags bis samstags von 14-20 Uhr”; free and anonymous.
sources.application: A children’s helpline gives a child someone to talk to who is not part of their family or church.
sources.limits: Germany; other countries have their own children’s lines.

sources.title: Digital Spiritual Formation in Post-Christian Europe
sources.author: Tobias Treppmann · Kairos University, 2026 (the editor’s own research)
sources.shows: Notes that an academic study of five AI Jesus platforms found none church-endorsed; that spiritual direction rests on the director’s own formation, empathy and accountability to a community; and that a companion tuned to agree becomes “spiritual comfort food”.
sources.application: Whatever role an assistant plays, it should not be built to agree; and no role replaces a person accountable to a community.
sources.limits: An analytical paper by the editor, not an effectiveness study; unpublished.

sources.title: Antiqua et nova: note on the relationship between artificial intelligence and human intelligence
sources.author: Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith and Dicastery for Culture and Education · 28 January 2025
sources.shows: AI “must be understood for what it is: a tool, not a person”; no AI can genuinely experience empathy; misrepresenting AI as a person “should always be avoided”; AI can only simulate relationships.
sources.application: Avoid persona and companion designs that present the assistant as someone who loves, feels or prays.
sources.limits: Catholic teaching document; other traditions reason differently, though widely in the same direction.

sources.title: Towards understanding sycophancy in language models
sources.author: Anthropic researchers · 2023
sources.shows: Studied assistants sometimes preferred agreement with user views over truthfulness.
sources.application: Test belief reversal, flattering moral endorsement and harmful agreement.
sources.limits: Specific studied models and tasks; not a faith-app intervention study.

review.what: The replies to a grieving child, to a child asking the AI to be their friend and to a child who is scared at home, the help offered and the place of parents in it, and the reflection on children’s questions
needs: theology across Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant traditions
